P21: My research for this article turned up no well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, with the whole sequence on record: the conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. Maybe the records are private, or the cases went elsewhere. Either way, I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review that the home community doesn't control.
P25b: They'll also need transferable skills and education, relationships outside the community, access to their own records and documents, and at least one plausible next step, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. It's great if the community has the resources to help with the transition, with temporary housing, travel, tools or a little money set aside, but even if it doesn't, it can still not punish anyone for leaving, and not hold back the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function out there. No upbringing gives you perfect freedom, and the point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
P27: Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Multiply that by twenty adults, each with their own childhood.
P28: Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once a child is already living inside the disagreement. There has to be enough common ground on how kids are raised that the community hangs together. And the parents still need room to be parents.
